---
title: "A Bootstrap Algorithm for Comparing Diagnostic Test Accuracy in Meta-Analysis"
body-classes: project-page
---

::: {.project-meta}
Manuscript in preparation · Aug 2026 – present · Department of Statistics, Jeonbuk National University
:::

When two diagnostic tests are compared across published studies, the quantity of
interest is the difference in areas under their summary ROC curves. The data
available for it are usually nothing richer than aggregated 2×2 tables. Many of
those studies are paired — the same participants took both tests — but the methods
in common use treat the two tests as independent, and that assumption costs more
than it looks.

## The problem

Ignoring the dependence between paired tests misrepresents the variability of the
estimated difference. Under the positive dependence typical of two tests applied
to the same participants, it produces confidence intervals that are wider than
they should be and loses power. Under negative dependence it does the opposite:
it understates the variability and inflates the type I error rate.

![The design the method is built for: one set of participants, both tests. Sensitivity is read off the diseased participants and specificity off the non-diseased ones, for each test in turn — so the two tests' results are not independent, which is exactly what an independence-based interval ignores.](images/fig-dauc-paired.jpg){fig-alt="Diagram of a paired diagnostic study: one group of diseased and non-diseased participants, each undergoing both tests"}

## Methods

The paper proposes a correlation-aware bootstrap. Both tests are embedded in a
four-variate random-effects model, and the within-study correlations — which
published studies almost never report — are set to a default value derived from
Fréchet bounds and Fisher's z-transformation. The procedure accommodates fully
paired, partially paired and unpaired studies, and needs no individual
participant data.

Monte Carlo simulations in R compare it against the independence-based bootstrap
across a range of within- and between-study correlations, recording type I error,
power, interval length and coverage.

## Findings

The proposed procedure gives type I error rates and interval lengths close to
those obtained with the true within-study correlations, and detects differences
between tests more often than the independence-based bootstrap when the tests are
dependent — particularly when the dependence also arises between studies. Where
no such dependence exists, the two procedures behave alike.

Three published diagnostic meta-analyses are reanalysed to illustrate the
procedure.
